entry.title: Talatat: Portrait of Nefertiti
entry.blurb: The son of Amenhotep III, Akhenaten, brought about the short-lived "monotheistic" revolution in Egyptian religion near the end of Dynasty 18.

source.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

facts: Even though all we see is a fragment of the head we know it is Nefertiti by the double uraeus or serpent symbol on the headband, which was only worn by the queen.
The young king constructed a temple complex to the Aten, the Sun Disk, at Karnak—from which this relief comes—before he moved his capital to El Armana.
For reasons yet unknown, the figure of the Queen Nefertiti appears in these reliefs far more often than that of the king.

candidate.title: Talatat: Portrait of Nefertiti
candidate.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art. Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
candidate.description: The son of Amenhotep III, Akhenaten, brought about the short-lived "monotheistic" revolution in Egyptian religion near the end of Dynasty 18. The young king constructed a temple complex to the Aten, the Sun Disk, at Karnak—from which this relief comes—before he moved his capital to El Armana. For reasons yet unknown, the figure of the Queen Nefertiti appears in these reliefs far more often than that of the king. Ironically, the Aten temples were dismantled anciently to be used as foundations and fill for additions to the Great Temple of Amun, whom the Aten had briefly displaced. Even though all we see is a fragment of the head we know it is Nefertiti by the double uraeus or serpent symbol on the headband, which was only worn by the queen.
